# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 7 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 7 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_007_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 2, Chapter 3

**1** Six young men who had accompanied her were constructing the tower. Thousands of other workers were bringing stones — some hauled up from the depths of the sea, others carried in from dry land — and handing them off to the six builders. **2** Every stone that came out of the sea was placed straight into the wall, just as it came, because these stones were smooth and fitted perfectly at the joints. They locked together so seamlessly that you couldn't find the seams, and the tower looked as if it had grown from a single stone. **3** The land-stones were sorted: some thrown away, some used, some broken to pieces and discarded far from the site. **4** Plenty of stones lay scattered around the tower. Some were not used. Some were thrown far away. Some were cracked. And some were white and round and simply would not fit into the wall no matter how they were tried. **5** I saw other stones flung far away. Some that hit the road didn't stay on it — they bounced off into rough, pathless ground. Some fell into fire and burned. Others landed near the water but couldn't roll in, even though they seemed to be straining toward it. **6** She was about to leave when I stopped her. "My lady, what's the point of seeing all this if you won't explain it to me?" She smiled at my persistence. "You're quite bold, wanting to know all about the tower." "Please tell me anyway." **7** "This tower," she said, "is the Church." "And who are the six young men building it?" "They are the holy angels of God — the first-created ones — to whom the Lord gave responsibility over all his creation, to build it up and govern it. They will complete the tower." **8** "And the thousands of other workers?" "Also holy angels of God. But the six are over them all. When the building is finished, they will all celebrate together around the tower and praise God for the completion of his work." **9** "Now please explain the stones to me," I said. She replied: "The white, square stones that fit perfectly at the joints — they are the apostles, bishops, teachers, and deacons who lived in God's holiness and served him faithfully and purely. Some have already died; others are still alive. They always agreed with one another and lived in peace, which is why they fit so precisely into the wall. **10** The stones from the sea — those who were dragged up from the deep — are the people who suffered for the name of the Lord." **11** "And the land-stones?" "Those are people who didn't suffer, but whose holy lives pleased God — people who kept the Lord's commandments." "And the rejected ones?" **12** "Those are people who have sinned but want to repent. That's why they haven't been thrown far — they can still be used if they turn around now. But they have to act quickly: repentance is only possible while the tower is still being built. Once it is finished, that door closes." **13** "And the cracked ones?" "These are the hypocrites — people who said they believed but never actually changed. Their wickedness remained. There is no salvation for them because they are no use to the building." **14** "And those white round ones that keep not fitting?" She shook her head. "How long will you keep being so slow? Those are the wealthy believers. They have faith, but they also have riches, and when trouble comes, they choose their money and their business over their Lord." "Will they ever fit into the building?" "When their wealth is stripped away — the wealth that's enchanted them — then yes. A round stone can't become a square one without losing something of itself. The same is true of the wealthy: they cannot be fit for God's use unless their riches are removed. **15** Think about yourself: when you were rich, you were useless to God. Now you are useful and you have real life. Take the lesson — you yourself were cut from this very stone."

---

*PNEUMA note: The image of round stones straining toward the water (v.5) is one of the Shepherd's most striking details — perhaps depicting souls who desire baptism but cannot attain it.*
